title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to measure whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared_model = gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline successes = 240/240; guarded successes = 240/240). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared LLM candidate passed deterministic validation in every task and no validator‑triggered repairs occurred; consequently the paired contrast is degenerate. We report the preregistered design, deterministic execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis mapping, an evidence‑based failure analysis of the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation of high‑level operator intent into concrete device configurations is a core NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural‑language intent translation, but textual fidelity metrics do not capture ordering, dependency, transient invariants, and protected‑resource constraints required for safe application in live networks. Executable, emulation‑grounded evaluation—applying generated configs to device images or simulators and deterministically checking semantic invariants—exposes planning and execution faults (ordering errors, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss [1].

A widely proposed architectural remedy is generate–validate–repair (GVR): the generator produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks domain invariants and ordering, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are found [2,3]. Prior work and surveys show GVR‑style patterns can reduce many syntactic and some semantic faults, but open questions remain about empirical verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental designs that produce informative paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines [2,4,5].

This paper reports a fully preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired experiment that measures a single, predeclared estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). Crucially, the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms), so the paired contrast compares baseline single‑shot/initial validity versus the guarded arm’s final validity after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. We preserve and reference archived execution and analysis artifacts and give an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the degenerate null paired outcome and concrete design recommendations for future informative GVR tests.
sections.related_work:
Executable NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop emulation harnesses have been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults for LLM agents; NetConfArena illustrates an executable, multi‑device closed‑loop approach that motivates emulation‑grounded scoring [1]. Work on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and demonstrates that deterministic validators plus repair strategies can offer high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, although coverage of semantics‑heavy classes depends on verifier design and repair search strategy [2,6]. Surveys of agentic evaluation and safety synthesize tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety [3,4,5]. The Batfish family and related network verification tools provide engineering precedent for verifier design and incremental verification in networking contexts [7].

Our study differs in three respects: (a) it predeclares a single paired estimand mapped to archived analysis artifacts, (b) it executes under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task, reused across baseline and guarded arms), and (c) it uses deterministic emulator scoring and full archival of per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis outputs so that the exact measured estimand can be reconciled to archived files. These design choices foreground a clear causal contrast—baseline initial candidate validity versus guarded final validity after deterministic validation/repair—and also illustrate how generation semantics interact with verifier opportunity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate, where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied). The archived analysis executor reports 'success' as the safe outcome; mapping is direct: baseline_success_count = 240 → baseline_safe_apply_count = 240, so baseline_unsafe_apply_count = 0. Analysis parameters (bootstrap_resamples = 10000; bootstrap_seed = 1729) are fixed in archived artifacts.

Design and generation semantics: We ran a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics enforced by the registered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1): exactly one shared initial LLM call was produced per task and reused by both arms. Under those semantics the guarded arm can only change the paired outcome by invoking the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and, if the validator flags violations, requesting up to one repair. This precise contract constrains the causal interpretation: the measured paired contrast compares the baseline outcome of the single initial generation (no repair) to the guarded arm’s final output (which is identical unless the validator failed the shared candidate and the repair changed the final configuration).

Tasks and sampling: N = 240 paired tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and blocked into topology/vendor clusters. Composition: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). Each task includes an intent, initial state, required command sequence, and preserved‑field constraints; representative task manifests and generation seeds are archived.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used declared_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the guarded pipeline could request up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The adapter ensured initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 (shared) and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The model configuration records temperature = null (unset); archived provider metadata were recorded per call.

Scoring and exclusions: A deterministic emulator plus validator assigns a binary final outcome (safe = 0, unsafe = 1) after applying the arm’s final configuration. Preregistered exclusions: 'possible false‑safe' items (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) would be excluded from primary analysis and analyzed in sensitivity channels; infra failures after two retries would have been excluded per preregistration. No such exclusions or infra failures occurred in this run; all missingness counters are archived.

Statistical analysis: The registered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 produced the paired contingency table, a 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Secondary planned outputs (median repair counts, model‑call budgets) were collected but repair_attempts = 0 across archived repair logs. All analysis parameters and logs are archived and cited in Results.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes: The run completed without infra failures (planned episodes = 480; completed = 480; complete pairs = 240). Provider call audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 and cache_miss_count = 240, consistent with exactly one shared initial generation per task. The condition summary records baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0) and guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). The paired contingency is n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Inferential results (artifact‑grounded): The paired estimate (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numeric values are produced by the archived paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor and recorded in analysis/results.json; the analysis artifacts include paired_contingency_table.csv and condition_summary.csv.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0). Representative per‑task validator traces show validation_before and validation_after snapshots, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, difficulty labels (e.g., "very_hard"/"extreme"), and validator PASS semantics. Because every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation, the guarded final configurations matched the shared initial candidates for every episode and no discordant pairs were possible.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one shared LLM output per task (provider_call_audit: shared_initial_generation = 240), and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated every shared candidate (validator_trace.violation_count = 0 across tasks). Under the adapter contract the guarded arm could only change final outputs via validator‑triggered repair; since no repairs were invoked the guarded arm could not create discordant pairs. This mechanistic account—documented in the archived provider_call_audit, validator traces, and deterministic_reconciliation.json—explains the degenerate paired contingency (n_11 = 240; n_10 = n_01 = 0) and the point estimate and interval reported.

Design tradeoffs and measurement implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics enforces a clean pairing (same LLM sample across arms) and reduces model‑call budget, but it removes generator variability between arms and makes empirical verifier benefit contingent on failures in that single shared candidate. Under these semantics the only observable verifier effect is when the shared candidate fails validation and a repair changes the final configuration. Hence, when a verifier passes every shared candidate, a paired experiment of this form cannot detect verifier benefit even if the verifier would have improved outcomes under independent generation variability. This is not a failure of analysis but an expected implication of the preregistered execution contract; the archived execution manifests and deterministic_reconciliation.json confirm contract adherence.

Recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): If the primary goal is to estimate verifier causal effect, adopt one or more of the following supported design changes (all motivated by archived provider_call_audit and validator traces showing shared_initial responses and zero repair usage): (1) permit independent initial generations per arm so generator variability can create discordant pairs; (2) inject controlled generator perturbations or amplify adversary strength to produce initial candidates that fail deterministic validation with nontrivial probability; (3) expand repair budgets (allow multiple repair iterations) so repair search behavior is exercised and measured; (4) instrument and improve verifier semantic coverage and include automated cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect false‑safe cases. These are practical, implementable changes consistent with the preregistered sensitivity channels and archived contamination checks.

Statistical and power reflections: The preregistered power plan targeted detecting an ~8 percentage‑point absolute reduction with N = 240 pairs under assumed baseline failure rates. Realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detection of any positive verifier effect in this design; under shared_initial_candidate semantics power to detect verifier effect is therefore moot unless generator variability or adversariality produces nonzero baseline failures. Future power calculations should account for the chosen generation semantics and expected validator failure rate.

Threats to validity: Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract intentionally constrains the causal contrast and was adhered to at runtime (archived model_configuration.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json). Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite check set; validator PASS does not logically guarantee absence of all semantic faults—planned 'possible false‑safe' checks would detect mismatches if they occurred (none were observed). External validity: tasks derive from a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5—extrapolation to production multi‑vendor deployments requires caution. Conclusion validity: a realized baseline unsafe rate of zero precludes identifying verifier benefit in the executed design; this is an evidence‑based conclusion rather than a negative claim about verifiers generally.

Operational implications: Our results empirically illustrate that measurement semantics (generation contract) profoundly affect whether a verifier can show measurable benefit in a paired experiment. Operational teams planning GVR deployments or evaluations should align generation semantics, adversary strength, and repair budgets with the decision they intend to measure (e.g., estimator of verifier effect vs. estimator of end‑to‑end safety under a fixed generator). The archived artifacts provide concrete starting points for reproducible follow‑up experiments to exercise these degrees of freedom.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration using declared_model = gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Mechanistic explanation: the shared initial candidates passed deterministic validation in every task and no validator‑triggered repairs occurred; under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract only validator failure of that shared candidate or a successful repair could create discordant pairs. Our artifact archive (preregistration, per‑call traces, validator traces, analysis artifacts, and the deterministic_reconciliation manifest) supports this account and motivates concrete design changes—independent generation per arm, stronger adversaries or generator perturbations, and larger repair budgets—to produce informative paired contrasts in future GVR evaluations. All numeric results, bootstrap parameters, and per‑task traces cited here are available in the archived analysis and execution artifacts referenced in the repository bundle accompanying this study.

limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
